title: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
summary: Bound any kernel by peak FLOP/s and memory bandwidth: compute arithmetic intensity and the ridge point, measure real bandwidth with a copy kernel, and place GEMM, softmax and LLM decode on an H100 roofline.
outcomes: Compute the arithmetic intensity of GEMM, GEMV and elementwise kernels from FLOP and byte counts
Explain why the ridge point decides whether a kernel is memory bound or compute bound
Measure achieved DRAM bandwidth with a copy kernel and avoid the cache, unit and warm-up traps
Predict why batch 1 LLM decode reaches well under 1 percent of H100 peak FLOP/s
Read a hierarchical roofline in Nsight Compute to judge cache reuse

lessons.title: Why a kernel is limited by its slowest resource

blocks.md:
A GPU datasheet advertises two headline numbers: how fast it can do math (FLOP/s, floating point operations per second) and how fast it can move data between its DRAM and the chip (bytes per second). A kernel needs both. It cannot finish before its math is done, and it cannot finish before its data has arrived.

We will use one GPU throughout: the **NVIDIA H100 SXM**. Its datasheet lists 3.35 TB/s of HBM3 memory bandwidth and 1,979 TFLOP/s of BF16 Tensor Core math, marked "with sparsity". Sparsity (2:4 structured) doubles the rated throughput, so ordinary dense BF16 math peaks at half of that: **989.5 TFLOP/s**.

In the previous course you saw how warps fetch memory in coalesced sectors. Now we zoom out and ask a coarser question: given how many FLOPs a kernel does and how many bytes it must move to and from DRAM, what is the best time it could possibly reach?

The simplest model assumes math and memory traffic overlap perfectly, so the kernel takes as long as the slower of the two.

blocks.caption: F is the FLOP count, Q the bytes moved to and from DRAM, P peak FLOP/s, B peak bandwidth. This is a lower bound on time, not a prediction.

blocks.prompt: A ReLU over 2^28 BF16 values does one operation per element and reads and writes 2 bytes per element. On an H100, roughly how does its math time compare to its memory time?
blocks.reveal: Math: 2^28 FLOP / 989.5 TFLOP/s = **0.27 us**. Memory: 4 bytes x 2^28 = 1.07 GB / 3.35 TB/s = **320.5 us**. Memory takes over 1,000 times longer. (Simplified: we used the Tensor Core peak, but ReLU runs on the regular cores; even at the 67 TFLOP/s FP32 peak its math takes only 4.0 us, still 80 times less than the memory time.) Making the math faster would change nothing; only moving fewer bytes helps.

blocks.title: Math time versus memory time on an H100 (BF16)

scenes.caption: ReLU on 2^28 BF16 values: even at Tensor Core speed, 0.27 us of math hides inside 320.5 us of memory traffic. The kernel is memory bound; the math units sit idle almost the whole time.
An 8192 x 8192 x 8192 BF16 GEMM: 1.1 TFLOP of math takes 1,111 us, while its 402.7 MB of minimum traffic needs only 120.2 us. Now math dominates: compute bound.
One decode step of a 4096 x 4096 linear layer at batch 1 (a GEMV): 0.034 us of math, 10.0 us to stream the 33.6 MB weight matrix. Memory bound by about 300 times.

blocks.md: The ratio that decides which side wins is **arithmetic intensity**: FLOPs performed divided by bytes moved, in FLOP/byte. NVIDIA's GPU Performance Background guide defines it exactly this way and compares it to the GPU's own ratio of math rate to memory bandwidth, which it calls the **ops:byte ratio**. If the kernel's intensity is below the GPU's ops:byte ratio, memory time is longer and the kernel is memory limited; above it, math limited.

A third limiter exists: latency. If a kernel launches too few threads to keep the GPU busy, it reaches neither the math peak nor the bandwidth peak. NVIDIA's guide lists "latency if there is not sufficient parallelism" as the likely limiter in that case. The max formula above assumes enough parallelism.

blocks.question: A kernel does 2 GFLOP and moves 4 GB on an H100 (989.5 TFLOP/s BF16, 3.35 TB/s). Which change would speed it up the most?
options: Switching from BF16 to FP8 Tensor Cores to double the math rate
Fusing it with the next kernel so its output never goes to DRAM
Raising the SM clock to increase peak FLOP/s
Unrolling the inner loop to improve instruction level parallelism
blocks.explain: Math time is 2 GFLOP / 989.5 TFLOP/s = 2 us, memory time is 4 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 1,194 us. The kernel is memory bound, so only cutting bytes (fusion keeps intermediates on chip) helps. Every option that speeds up math leaves the 1,194 us untouched.

blocks.question: Kernel X has intensity 50 FLOP/byte and kernel Y has 500 FLOP/byte. The GPU's ops:byte ratio is about 295. What can you conclude?
options: Both are compute bound because 50 and 500 are both much larger than 1
X is compute bound and Y is memory bound
X is memory bound; Y can be compute bound if it has enough parallelism
Neither, because intensity says nothing without the clock frequency
blocks.explain: Compare each intensity to the machine ratio, not to 1. 50 is below 295, so memory time dominates for X. 500 is above 295, so Y's math time dominates, provided enough threads run to reach the peak at all.

lessons.title: The roofline: attainable FLOP/s versus intensity

blocks.md: Williams, Waterman and Patterson turned the max formula into a picture in their 2008 Berkeley report, published in Communications of the ACM in 2009. Divide both sides of the time bound by F and invert it, and you get the best performance any kernel with intensity $I = F/Q$ can attain on a given machine.

blocks.caption: The paper's form: Attainable GFlops/sec = Min(Peak Floating Point Performance, Peak Memory Bandwidth x Operational Intensity).

blocks.md:
On a log-log plot with intensity on the x axis and FLOP/s on the y axis, $B \times I$ is a straight sloped line and $P_{\text{peak}}$ is a flat line. Together they form a roof. Any kernel's achieved performance must sit under that roof at its own x position.

The two lines meet at the **ridge point**, at $I^{*} = P_{\text{peak}} / B_{\text{peak}}$. The paper puts it plainly: the ridge point's x coordinate is the minimum intensity needed to reach maximum performance. For the H100 in dense BF16 that is 989.5 / 3.35 = **295.4 FLOP/byte**.

blocks.title: Roofline of an H100 SXM (drag peak and bandwidth)

scenes.caption: Dense BF16 on Tensor Cores: 989.5 TFLOP/s and 3.35 TB/s put the ridge at 295.4 FLOP/byte. A batch 1 GEMV at 1 FLOP/byte can reach at most 3.35 TFLOP/s, 0.34 percent of peak.

Same chip, FP64 on the regular cores: 34 TFLOP/s per the datasheet. The ridge falls to 10.1 FLOP/byte, so far more kernels can reach the FP64 peak. The ridge depends on the precision and unit, not just the chip.
Hypothetical: keep 989.5 TFLOP/s but raise bandwidth to 5 TB/s. The slope moves up and the ridge drops to 197.9 FLOP/byte. More bandwidth helps only kernels left of the ridge.
Hypothetical: keep 3.35 TB/s and double math to 1979 TFLOP/s. The ridge moves right to 590.7 FLOP/byte. Memory bound kernels gain nothing, and fewer kernels can reach the new peak.

blocks.md: The ridge point tells you how hard the machine is to feed. The paper notes that a ridge far to the right means only kernels with very high intensity can reach peak. From the V100 (138.9) to the H100 in BF16 (295.4), the ridge more than doubled.

scenes.caption: The paper's 2008 Opteron X2: 17.6 GFLOP/s peak and 15 GB/s measured, a ridge of 1.17 (the paper rounds it to 1.0). The H100 FP64 ridge is 10.1; V100 (125 TFLOP/s, about 900 GB/s) is 138.9; H100 BF16 is 295.4.

blocks.md: Terminology: the original paper says **operational intensity** and counts only DRAM traffic after the caches have filtered it. NVIDIA's docs and Nsight Compute say **arithmetic intensity**. In this course the two mean the same thing unless we name a cache level explicitly.

blocks.question: A vendor releases a GPU with twice the Tensor Core FLOP/s of its predecessor and the same memory bandwidth. Which kernel speeds up the most?
options: A batch 1 GEMV at 1 FLOP/byte
A softmax at about 1 FLOP/byte
A large square GEMM at about 1,365 FLOP/byte
All three speed up by the same 2x
blocks.explain: Doubling the flat roof only raises kernels to the right of the old ridge. The GEMV and softmax sit on the sloped bandwidth line, which did not move, so they gain nothing. Only the high intensity GEMM can climb to the new, higher roof.

blocks.question: On the H100 in dense BF16, a kernel with intensity 100 FLOP/byte achieves 200 TFLOP/s. How close is it to its roofline bound?
options: At 20 percent of the bound, since the peak is 989.5 TFLOP/s
At about 60 percent of the bound, which is 335 TFLOP/s
Above the bound, so the measurement must be wrong
Exactly at the bound because 100 is below the ridge
blocks.explain: Left of the ridge the bound is B x I = 3.35 x 100 = 335 TFLOP/s, not the flat peak. 200 / 335 is about 60 percent. Comparing to 989.5 overstates the gap, because no kernel at intensity 100 can reach that height.

lessons.title: Measuring achieved bandwidth with a copy kernel

blocks.md: The roofline is only as good as its two numbers. The paper did not take bandwidth from the DRAM spec: the authors wrote progressively optimized microbenchmarks to find **sustainable** DRAM bandwidth, which they describe as the steady state bandwidth of the memory system, not the pin bandwidth of the DRAM chips. The same advice applies to GPUs.
The CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide shows how the theoretical number is built from hardware specs. A V100 has HBM2 at an 877 MHz memory clock on a 4096-bit interface, double data rate:

blocks.caption: The guide notes the same value is 836.4 GiB/s if you divide by 1024^3 instead of 10^9. Use the same divisor for theory and measurement.
From the CUDA guide: bytes read plus bytes written by the kernel, divided by the measured time in seconds.

blocks.md: A copy kernel `c[i] = a[i]` is the cleanest probe: it does no math, reads each byte of `a` once and writes each byte of `c` once, so $B_r + B_w$ is exactly two arrays. BabelStream, the GPU take on the STREAM benchmark from the University of Bristol, does exactly this. By default it uses 33,554,432 doubles per array (268.4 MB), counts Copy as 2 arrays moved, repeats each kernel 100 times and ignores the first run.

blocks.title: Timing a copy kernel and computing GB/s

scenes.caption: A grid-stride loop, the same shape as BabelStream's CUDA copy kernel. Consecutive threads touch consecutive doubles, so every warp access is fully coalesced.
Count bytes from the algorithm, not from a profiler: one read and one write per element. Each array is 268.4 MB, far larger than the H100's 50 MB L2, so the data really comes from HBM.
Run once untimed. The first launch can include one-time startup costs that are not bandwidth; BabelStream likewise discards its first iteration.
CUDA events bracket the second launch on the GPU timeline. Synchronize on the stop event before reading the elapsed time. Suppose it reports 0.180 ms (an illustrative value).
536.9 MB / 0.180 ms = 2,982.6 GB/s, which is 89.0 percent of the 3.35 TB/s datasheet figure. Repeat many times and report the best or median, not one run.

blocks.md: Real measurements land below the datasheet. The Empirical Roofline Toolkit (ERT) from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, as extended by Yang, Wang, Farrell, Kurth and Williams, measured **828.8 GB/s** of HBM bandwidth on a V100 rated at about 900 GB/s, and 103.7 TFLOP/s on its Tensor Cores against the 125 TFLOP/s headline (the paper puts it at 96.5 percent of the theoretical peak for those GPUs). Build your roofline from measured ceilings like these, or you will think kernels are further from the roof than they can ever get.

blocks.title: V100 HBM2 bandwidth: three different numbers

scenes.caption: The rounded datasheet figure (900), the CUDA guide's formula (898) and a tuned microbenchmark (828.8, 92 percent of 900). The measured number is the real roof for your kernels.

blocks.md:
Common traps:
- **Arrays that fit in L2.** An 8 MB array on an H100 (50 MB L2) measures cache bandwidth, not HBM.
- **Mixing GB and GiB.** 2,982.6 GB/s is 2,777.8 GiB/s. Use one divisor for both theory and measurement.
- **Timing the first launch** or using host timers without synchronizing.
- **Uncoalesced or strided access**, which measures your access pattern, not the memory.

Which tool? The CUDA samples once shipped `bandwidthTest`, but its changelog for CUDA 12.9 removes it as out of date and points to [NVBandwidth](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvbandwidth), which measures copies across links (host to device, GPU to GPU) with copy engines or SM kernels. For on-device HBM bandwidth, a STREAM-style kernel such as [BabelStream](https://github.com/UoB-HPC/BabelStream) is the direct analog of the paper's microbenchmarks.

blocks.question: A colleague times a copy of two 4 MB float arrays on an H100 and reports 6 TB/s, far above the 3.35 TB/s datasheet. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The datasheet understates HBM3 bandwidth for float data
The arrays fit in the 50 MB L2, so the copy measured cache bandwidth
They forgot to count the write, so the number should be doubled
Coalesced access lets HBM exceed its rated bandwidth
blocks.explain: After the warm-up run, 8 MB of data sits in the 50 MB L2, so the timed run is served mostly from cache. Arrays must be many times larger than the last level cache. Forgetting the write would make the result too low, not too high.

blocks.question: Your Triad kernel a[i] = b[i] + s * c[i] on 2^25 doubles takes 0.30 ms. What effective bandwidth do you report?
options: 1,789.6 GB/s, counting only the two arrays read
894.8 GB/s, counting one array
2,684.4 GB/s, counting two reads and one write
3,579.1 GB/s, counting four arrays
blocks.explain: Triad reads b and c and writes a: three arrays of 268.4 MB, 805.3 MB total. 805.3 MB / 0.30 ms = 2,684.4 GB/s. BabelStream gives Triad a weight of 3 for exactly this reason.

lessons.title: Placing GEMM, softmax and LLM decode on the roofline

blocks.md: To place a kernel, count its FLOPs and its minimum DRAM bytes. NVIDIA's Matrix Multiplication Background guide does this for a GEMM of an M x K matrix by a K x N matrix: it needs M N K fused multiply-adds, 2 M N K FLOPs, and at minimum reads both inputs and writes the output once. With 2-byte (FP16 or BF16) elements:

blocks.caption: This is the best case: each element moved once. Real kernels move somewhat more, so real intensity is a little lower.

blocks.md:
For a square GEMM with M = N = K this is simply $N/3$. So on the H100 (ridge 295.4):

- 512 x 512 x 512: intensity 170.7, bound 571.7 TFLOP/s (memory side).
- 1024 x 1024 x 1024: 341.3, just past the ridge.
- 8192 x 8192 x 8192: 2,730.7, comfortably compute bound.
- 8192 x 128 x 8192: 124.1, which the guide calls memory limited even on a V100 (ridge 138.9). One thin dimension drags intensity down.

blocks.prompt: During LLM decode, each new token multiplies its activation vector by every weight matrix. For a 4096 x 4096 BF16 layer at batch size 1, what is the intensity?
blocks.reveal: FLOPs: 2 x 4096 x 4096 = 33.6 M. Bytes: the 4096 x 4096 weight matrix is 33.6 MB, plus two tiny 8 KB vectors. Intensity is about **1 FLOP/byte**. NVIDIA's guide makes the same point: matrix-vector products (M = 1 or N = 1) have intensity less than 1 and are always memory limited. Its table lists a batch 1 linear layer at 1 FLOP/B.

blocks.md: Batching changes everything because the weights are read once and reused for every token in the batch. With batch size b and a square d x d layer, intensity is $b\,d/(d + 2b)$, roughly $b$ when b is much smaller than d. Drag the sliders to see where decode stops being memory bound.

blocks.title: A d x d BF16 linear layer: attainable TFLOP/s vs batch

scenes.caption: H100 BF16, d = 4096. Batch 1 reaches at most 3.35 TFLOP/s; batch 64 reaches 207.9. The layer only becomes compute bound at about 345 tokens per step.
d = 8192 barely moves the crossover (about 318). For small batches, intensity is set by the batch, not the layer size: the weights dominate the bytes either way.
Hypothetical 5 TB/s part with the same math: batch 1 rises to 5.0 TFLOP/s and the crossover drops to about 219. For small batch decode, bandwidth is the spec that matters.

blocks.md: This explains a rule of thumb for single-stream generation. A model with 7 billion BF16 parameters holds 14 GB of weights, and every decode step must read all of them. At 3.35 TB/s that takes at least 4.18 ms, so batch 1 decode is capped near **239 tokens per second** on one H100, no matter how fast the Tensor Cores are. (Simplified: this ignores KV cache reads, which only add bytes.)

blocks.title: Roofline bound as percent of H100 BF16 peak

scenes.caption: Upper bounds from min(989.5, 3.35 x I), each as a share of 989.5 TFLOP/s. Only shapes past the 295.4 ridge can reach 100 percent; real kernels land below these bounds.

blocks.md: Elementwise and normalization kernels sit far left. NVIDIA's guide lists ReLU at 0.25 FLOP/byte (one operation per 2 bytes read and 2 written) and layer normalization at under 10, both memory limited. It classes softmax as a reduction that is typically memory limited. A rough count of 5 operations per element (max, subtract, exp, sum, divide) over 4 bytes in and out gives about 1.25 FLOP/byte for a fused single pass. That is why these ops are fused into neighbors: fusion removes bytes, which is the only lever left of the ridge.

Intensity is not fixed for a given operation. It depends on shape (thin GEMMs fall left), precision (FP8 halves the bytes per element and so doubles intensity), and how well the implementation reuses data. A naive GEMM that rereads inputs from DRAM can be memory bound even at 8192 cubed.

blocks.question: A serving team raises decode batch size from 8 to 64 on a 4096-wide BF16 layer on an H100. Roughly what happens to the time per decode step for that layer?
options: It grows about 8x because there is 8x more math
It stays nearly the same, because the step is still bound by reading the weights
It halves because Tensor Cores are used more efficiently
It grows about 64x because each token needs its own weight read
blocks.explain: At batch 8 and 64 the layer is far left of the ridge (intensity about 8 and 62). Time is set by streaming 33.6 MB of weights, which is the same for both batches. Throughput rises almost 8x for free, which is why servers batch decode requests.

lessons.title: Ceilings, hierarchical rooflines and Nsight Compute

blocks.md: The roof is a bound you cannot cross. The paper adds **ceilings** below it: lower lines you cannot break through without a specific optimization. For their Opteron X2 the compute ceilings were 8.8 GFLOP/s with an unbalanced multiply and add mix and 2.2 GFLOP/s without ILP or SIMD as well. Memory ceilings were 11 GB/s without software prefetching, 4.8 GB/s without memory affinity as well, and 2.7 GB/s with only unit stride access.

The gap between one ceiling and the next is the reward for that optimization, and a kernel's intensity tells you which ceilings to look at. On a GPU the analogous ceilings are things like FP32 cores versus Tensor Cores (two flat roofs at very different heights) and coalesced versus strided loads (two slopes).

The classic roofline counts only DRAM bytes. A **hierarchical roofline** draws one sloped roof per memory level (L1, L2, HBM) and plots one point per level for the same kernel, each with its own intensity: FLOPs divided by the bytes moved at that level. Charlene Yang's NERSC work describes it as the extension of roofline to the whole memory hierarchy, used to understand cache reuse and data locality.

blocks.title: Hierarchical roofline for a 100 GFLOP kernel (V100 Tensor Core)

scenes.caption: Simplified model using NVIDIA's V100 figures (125 TFLOP/s, about 900 GB/s HBM, 3.1 TB/s L2). 5 GB of L2 traffic gives L2 intensity 20, bound 62 TFLOP/s; HBM intensity 200 is past its ridge. L2 is the limiter.
A streaming kernel: L2 and HBM traffic are both 2 GB, so both points sit at 50. HBM bounds it at 45 TFLOP/s. Points close together mean data is not reused in cache.

Back to the first kernel, now with better shared memory tiling: L2 traffic falls to 2.5 GB, L2 intensity rises to 40 and its bound to 124 TFLOP/s, right under the 125 peak. Same FLOPs, same HBM bytes.

blocks.md: Read the gaps. In the NERSC DeepCAM study, a kernel whose L1, L2 and HBM points sit close together shows a streaming pattern with poor cache locality; a large gap between the L2 and HBM points shows that L2 misses were rare. The binding level is the one whose roof is lowest at that level's own intensity.

Nsight Compute draws these charts for you. Its Profiling Guide describes the parts: a log scale FLOP/s axis, a log scale arithmetic intensity axis, a **memory bandwidth boundary** (the slope), a **peak performance boundary** (the flat part), the **ridge point** where they meet, and an **achieved value** for the profiled kernel. The distance from the achieved point up to the roof is the room for improvement. Hierarchical variants exist for double, single and half precision and for Tensor Cores.

blocks.code:
# Overview roofline for every kernel in the app
ncu --section SpeedOfLight_RooflineChart -o report ./app

# Hierarchical (L1, L2, DRAM) roofline for Tensor Core kernels
ncu --section SpeedOfLight_HierarchicalTensorRooflineChart -o report ./app

# Everything, including all roofline sections
ncu --set full -o report ./app
blocks.caption: Section identifiers from the Nsight Compute Profiling Guide. Open the .ncu-rep report in the Nsight Compute UI to see the charts.

blocks.md: Know what a roofline cannot tell you. NVIDIA's matrix guide calls the intensity comparison a simplified rule of thumb that ignores non-math instructions and the on-chip hierarchy. It also ignores latency limits (too little parallelism), tile and wave quantization (in the guide's A100 example, a 9-tile tail wave after a full 108-tile wave takes nearly as long as the full wave), and launch overhead for tiny kernels. A kernel far below the roof is a prompt to look for one of these, not proof that the roof is wrong.

blocks.question: Nsight Compute shows a kernel's L1, L2 and DRAM points almost on top of each other, sitting on the DRAM slope. What is the best next step?
options: Switch to Tensor Cores to raise the flat roof
Nothing: being on the DRAM roof means it is already optimal
Raise the clock frequency to move the ridge point left
Restructure for reuse (tiling, fusion) so fewer bytes reach DRAM
blocks.explain: Overlapping points mean almost every byte touched in L1 also came from DRAM: no reuse. The kernel is on the DRAM roof at its current intensity, so the way up is to raise intensity by reusing data in shared memory or registers, or by fusing with neighbors. A higher flat roof does nothing for a memory bound kernel.

blocks.question: A kernel at intensity 400 FLOP/byte on the H100 reaches only 150 TFLOP/s in BF16. Which explanation fits the roofline picture?
options: It is memory bound, because 150 is less than 3.35 x 400
It is compute side but far below the flat roof, so suspect too little parallelism, quantization or a non-Tensor Core path
The measurement must be wrong, since kernels right of the ridge always reach peak
Its intensity must actually be below 1
blocks.explain: 400 is right of the 295.4 ridge, so the bound is the 989.5 TFLOP/s flat roof. Being at 15 percent of it points at in-core issues: not enough tiles to fill the SMs, wave quantization, or math running on regular cores instead of Tensor Cores. Right of the ridge, reaching peak is possible, not guaranteed.
